messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 65
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Retail Worker
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 60

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Stay Near Exit: make sure to stay close to exit, Distraction: I distract myself with something else, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
  Negative Appraisals: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kofi Mensah is a 65-year-old Ghanaian-born man who has lived in the United States for nearly three decades, working for the past eleven years as a floor associate at a large home-improvement retail store in suburban Georgia. He came to the intake appointment accompanied by his wife, Abena, who sat quietly in the waiting room while Kofi spoke with measured, careful words about what had happened to him — and about what had not stopped happening since.

In the late summer of two years ago, Kofi was visiting family in coastal Louisiana when Hurricane Ida made landfall. He had stayed behind with his brother-in-law to protect the property, both men certain the storm would weaken before it arrived. It did not. The hours that followed were unlike anything Kofi had encountered in sixty-three years of living: the walls of his brother-in-law's house groaning and then partially giving way, floodwater rising past his knees and then his waist in near-total darkness, the roar of wind so absolute it swallowed every other sound. For several hours he clung to an interior door frame, unable to see more than inches in front of him, uncertain whether the structure above him would hold or collapse entirely. When the water finally receded enough for him to move, he found his brother-in-law injured but alive on the second floor. Both men were rescued the following morning. Kofi flew home to Georgia four days later with dry clothes and, as he described it to his therapist, "something broken inside that I cannot find to fix."

In the weeks after his return, Kofi noticed that the memories of those hours would not stay in the past where he placed them. They arrived without warning — not as recollections but as re-immersions, a film that did not merely play but pulled him back into the dark water, the groaning walls, the sensation of not knowing whether the next moment would be his last. During these episodes he was certain, in a way that no amount of reassurance could reach, that it was happening right now. Abena would find him rigid at the kitchen table, his hands gripping the edge, and he would be unable to explain to her that he was not in Georgia at all.

He had come to believe, with a quiet but unshakeable conviction, that the world had revealed its true nature to him that night — that it was irreducibly dangerous, that safety was an arrangement that could dissolve in hours, and that the man he had been before the storm was gone. He did not say this dramatically; he said it the way a person states a fact they have verified repeatedly. He was also certain that he had to remain alert at all times, that dropping his guard even briefly was an invitation to catastrophe.

This certainty reorganised his daily life in ways that accumulated over months. At the retail store where he works, Kofi now positions himself instinctively near the emergency exit at the far end of the lumber aisle — his assigned section — and he has quietly rearranged his work patterns so that he is rarely more than a few steps from that door. When customers approach him, he finds himself scanning the high ceiling, the wide concrete floor, the loading bay doors, cataloguing what might give way and what might hold. He falls asleep with difficulty most nights, feeling that unconsciousness itself is a form of exposure, a dropping of the watch he believes he must keep. He has begun declining invitations to family gatherings held in unfamiliar buildings, and Abena has noticed that he will not sit with his back to a room. A younger colleague at the store mentioned to a supervisor that Kofi seemed distracted and difficult to reach; Kofi received a quiet word about customer engagement that he found humiliating and that deepened his sense that the damage in him was permanent and visible to others.

What finally brought him to seek help was Abena's direct and tearful request one evening, after she found him standing at their bedroom window at two in the morning, scanning the yard. He came, he said, for her. What he feared most was that therapy would confirm what he already suspected — that there was no going back. What he hoped for, almost against his own belief, was to be wrong about that.
